statements.text: I wonder, I've been thinking a lot about the melding of our AI research with quantum that has the potential—really revolutionary potential. Would we fall behind in that critical area?
statements.context: House Science Committee hearing on the NSF FY2024 budget proposal.

statements.text: At the same time, AI technology is moving so fast that I worry voluntary guardrails will be too little too late. I recognize that NIST is not a regulatory agency so there are limits to the discussion we can have in this context, but we can still look to NIST for their deep technical expertise in informing our debates about policy.
statements.context: House Science Committee hearing on the NIST FY 2024 budget request, featuring NIST Director Dr. Laurie Locascio.

statements.text: I believe that AI is going to upend a lot of careers. In fact, the House of Representatives has had three bipartisan, Congress-wide briefings on AI in the last two weeks. It's going to upend the practice of law. It's going to upend the practice of medicine. It will probably upend engineering.
statements.context: House Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI and intellectual property, focusing on interoperability of AI and copyright law.

statements.text: I actually dislike the word trustworthy AI because it imparts to AI something that it doesn't have, human qualities.
statements.context: House committee hearing on artificial intelligence where Representative Obernolte questions witnesses on defining AI trustworthiness for legislative purposes.

statements.text: the idea that we would have a licensing regime, I think, is very daunting, as opposed to a registration regime where we might have the capacity for third parties to do auditing and the like.
statements.context: House hearing titled 'Artificial Intelligence: Advancing Innovation Towards the National Interest,' where Rep. Lofgren questions witnesses on regulatory design and compute concentration.

statements.text: What techniques are possible to identify copyrighted material in the training corpus of the large language models? Is it even possible to go back and identify protected material?
statements.context: House committee hearing on AI where Rep. Lofgren questions a witness about detecting copyrighted content in LLM training data.

statements.text: Can you highlight any examples of these biases and resulting consequences? And do you have thoughts on what are some of the more worrying implications of the use of AI and machine learning in law enforcement that would inform our thinking in terms of what we might do to set guardrails and prevent harm?
statements.context: House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology Members' Day hearing.

statements.text: It is important that we take steps more urgently on that given the artificial intelligence is already here. People are going to need to take action to protect their appearance and their personhood in AI. We don't have a statute I think in mind yet. I would very much welcome and ask for your assistance in crafting something that would provide that protection, but more importantly, that would think through how we might give people an easy avenue to enforce that right, because AI is massive. It is here. It is not going to be stopped. Yet, the potential for people to have their personhood misused is real, already here.
statements.context: House Oversight Subcommittee hearing on the U.S. Copyright Office, where Rep. Zoe Lofgren asks witnesses about legislating protections for individuals' likeness against AI misuse.

statements.text: do you want a single agency that we expect to know everything about every law, or do you want to enhance the capability of existing agencies that have expertise in an area of law to apply that in AI? [...] And I think, personally, the latter is likely to be successful.
statements.context: House hearing on AI risk management where Rep. Lofgren questions witnesses about regulatory architecture and developer accountability.

statements.text: I believe regulation of AI will be necessary, but I am also keenly aware that we must strike a balance that allows for innovation and ensures the U.S. maintains leadership.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren at a joint House Science Subcommittee hearing on AI risk management and governance.

statements.text: The goal of NAIRR is to democratize access to AI tools.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Zoe Lofgren at a House Science Committee hearing on federal science agencies and AI in scientific discovery.

statements.text: I don't think you have to be opposed to the private sector to believe, as I do, that this should not be owned by the biggest companies in the world. This should be open to startups. It should be open to researchers, not just the big companies.
statements.context: Congressional hearing on federal science agencies and AI's role in scientific discovery.

statements.text: The second thing is the confluence of several emerging technologies with dual-use potential, including AI, biotech, and quantum.
statements.context: Opening remarks at a House Science, Space, and Technology Committee oversight hearing on federal research-security implementation.

statements.text: I have a question about [...] how are we thinking about using AI if at all? [...] But it occurs to me that there may be a greater capability with AI. I'm wondering what each of you thinks about that. And then also, how do we deal with the persistent problem of hallucinations?
statements.context: House Science Committee hearing on U.S. competitiveness in weather forecasting and modeling.

statements.text: For example, Google unfolded every protein in the human body and posted it for every scientist in the world to use.
statements.context: House Judiciary Committee hearing on AI and intellectual property, focusing on IP protection for AI-assisted inventions and creative works.

statements.text: Because I believe that if there was infringement on the data collection for learning, there ought to be compensation, but I do worry if there were injunctive relief so that AI in America was enjoined, that would put us at a tremendous disadvantage versus China and others.
statements.context: House Judiciary Committee hearing on AI and intellectual property, focusing on IP protection for AI-assisted inventions and creative works.

statements.text: AI is going to provide tremendous tools for new things that are— obviously there are risks that we need to be aware of and prevent—but it is also a tremendous tool for good.
statements.context: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet hearing on radio, music, and copyrights, focused on recording artists' rights and AI-assisted music creation.

statements.text: If we handcuff the scientific arm of the EPA, we will discover the consequences of pesticide exposure the hard way—through impact on people who have been exposed. [...] It doesn’t matter how powerful the AI models are if they are based on unreliable or missing data. [...] Using AI to approve new chemicals without the critically necessary scientific health data to ensure they are safe is not innovation. It is recklessness.
statements.context: Opening statement by Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren at a House Environment Subcommittee hearing on AI in agrichemicals.

statements.text: I would just like to say that we ought to be working on a bipartisan basis again. The Science Committee staff task force, I would urge the speaker and whatever influence the Chair can have to reestablish that AI task force as a super Subcommittee of the Science Committee, so that we can get more work done, and get to where we need to be to have the guardrails and the standards that are appropriate at a national level.
statements.context: House Science Committee hearing on national AI strategy and state-level regulation, with witness testimony and member statements.

statements.text: If—if I may, Mr.—Mr. Kratsios, yes, the GSA is doing this, but we are essentially paying Musk. And we're going to have a problem here. I mean, inevitably, there's going to be a misuse. But even if we fire Federal employees who create pornography using Grok, that we would be paying Mr. Musk until he creates a barrier to this misuse is very troubling to me.
statements.context: Verbatim remarks by Rep. Zoe Lofgren during a hearing on advancing America's AI Action Plan.

statements.text: However, AI has also accelerated harmful and even criminal activities. Just a little over a week ago, xAI’s chatbot Grok made headlines by generating thousands of instances of nonconsensual sexual imagery – including child pornography – at the request of users on X’s main platform. We have also seen major instances of chatbots encouraging users with mental health issues to murder and commit suicide.
statements.context: Opening statement by Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren at a Research and Technology Subcommittee hearing on the Administration's AI Action Plan.

statements.text: Second, I am deeply concerned by the Administration taking cuts of revenue or equity in companies. The AI Action Plan emphasizes free markets, deregulation, and getting government out of the way of the private sector. But over the past year, the Administration has spent billions of taxpayer dollars to take direct ownership stakes in private companies. The government now owns nearly 10 percent of Intel, making it the largest shareholder. It holds equity positions in rare earth mining companies and is negotiating similar deals with quantum computing companies. This trend is unusual and concerning.
statements.context: Congressional hearing on the Administration's AI Action Plan, featuring testimony from CTO Michael Kratsios.

statements.text: AI has the potential to reshape the American economy and innovation ecosystem. I'm really excited about its promise and the potential opportunity it brings to improve productivity and to accelerate innovation. However, AI has also sometimes accelerated harmful and even criminal activities. [...] We've also seen major instances of chatbots encouraging users with mental health issues to murder and commit suicide.
statements.context: Congressional hearing on the Administration's AI Action Plan.

statements.text: more data and more transparency about data center impacts is essential. Communities should not have to make decisions about whether to host a data center without access to basic information about electricity usage, water consumption, air quality, noise pollution, and the potential effect on energy prices.
statements.context: Opening statement by Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren at a House Investigations and Oversight Subcommittee hearing on data center infrastructure for AI.

statements.text: We have discussed the ruling in California, fair use, essentially finding that data for training models is transformative, nonexpressive and, therefore, protected. Reasonable argument can be made on the other side. Meanwhile, we are not doing much here. [...] The question is, would Congress by rule or could the Executive by rule, or do we need to by rule enhance that opportunity for people to take technological steps to protect themselves from the Hoovering up of data?
statements.context: House IP Subcommittee hearing on internet and intellectual-property policy, where a member asks panelists about legislative options to protect personal data from AI training-data collection.

statements.text: If a human author is using AI to create, then they should have protection. Where do you draw the line between it is AI-generated and it is a human using AI as a tool?
statements.context: House IP subcommittee hearing on copyright and the internet, where Representative Lofgren questions a professor about AI and authorship.
